title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 2
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Box That Rebuilt Trade
passages.text:
A. Before the 1950s, cargo crossed the world in a form that had barely changed in centuries. Goods arrived at a port as barrels, sacks, crates and loose bundles, and were loaded piece by piece by gangs of dockworkers. A ship could spend longer in port being loaded and unloaded than it spent at sea. The cost of this labour, not the cost of the voyage, was the dominant expense in moving goods between continents.

B. The innovation usually credited to an American trucking operator in 1956 was not the metal box itself, which had precedents. It was the insight that the box was pointless unless everything around it changed too. A container is only efficient if cranes, ships, lorries, railway wagons and port layouts are all built to the same dimensions, and if the box is never opened between origin and destination. The idea being sold was a system, and the box was merely its most visible component.

C. Standardisation therefore mattered more than any engineering advance, and it was slow, contested and unglamorous. Competing operators had adopted incompatible sizes, each with sunk investment in equipment matched to their own. The agreements that eventually fixed international dimensions in the 1960s were negotiated rather than discovered, and several technically superior proposals lost to arrangements that more existing equipment already fitted.

D. The consequences for ports were severe and are frequently described as if they were unforeseeable. They were not. Container handling required deep water, large flat areas for stacking, and rail and road connections — conditions that old city-centre docks, hemmed in by centuries of building, could not provide. Trade shifted to new sites downstream or to entirely different cities, and dock labour forces that had numbered tens of thousands fell to hundreds within a generation.

E. What is harder to see is the effect on what gets made where. When moving goods was expensive, factories located near either their materials or their customers. As transport costs fell toward insignificance, that constraint weakened, and production could relocate to wherever labour and land were cheapest without the saving being consumed by freight. The container did not cause globalisation, but it removed a friction that had limited it, and the pattern of world manufacturing that followed is not easily imagined without it.

F. Economists studying the period have found the measurable effect on trade volumes larger than that of the trade agreements signed over the same decades — a finding that is regularly quoted and less regularly examined, since separating the two is difficult and the container's adoption was not random. What is not disputed is the direction: a mundane piece of steel changed the geography of production more than most policies designed to do so.

passages.title: The Unreliable Witness
passages.text:
Testimony from someone who saw an event is among the most persuasive evidence available to a court, and among the least reliable. This combination — high confidence, high persuasiveness, moderate accuracy — has been documented for more than a century, and the gap between how juries weigh such testimony and how well it performs remains one of the more consequential findings psychology has produced.

Memory does not work in the way the legal process implicitly assumes. It is not a recording that can be replayed with varying clarity. It is reconstructive: each act of recall assembles an account from fragments, and the assembly is influenced by what the person has learned, been asked and inferred since the event. This means a memory can change through the act of remembering it, and that repeated questioning does not simply retrieve the same material again.

The most robust experimental finding concerns misinformation. Where a witness encounters incorrect detail after an event — in a leading question, a news report, or conversation with another witness — that detail is frequently incorporated into the subsequent account and reported with the same confidence as accurate material. The witness is not lying and cannot distinguish the two. Investigators have therefore moved toward interviewing witnesses separately and toward question wording that avoids supplying detail, which is a change in procedure rather than in the witnesses.

Confidence is the element that most misleads courts. Jurors treat a confident witness as more accurate, and the correlation between confidence and accuracy, while positive, is far weaker than that assumption requires. Confidence is also malleable: a witness told that another witness identified the same person becomes markedly more confident without becoming more accurate, and that inflated confidence persists into testimony.

Identification across ethnic groups shows a consistent and well-replicated effect: people are on average better at distinguishing faces from a group they have substantial experience of than from one they do not. The effect is not evidence of prejudice and appears to reflect exposure, but its practical consequence in cross-ethnic identification cases is significant and is rarely explained to juries.

Reform has followed the evidence unevenly. Sequential rather than simultaneous presentation of suspects, administrators who do not know which person is the suspect, and recording a witness's confidence at the moment of first identification are all supported and unevenly adopted. The obstacle is not disagreement about the findings. It is that the procedures already in place produced convictions that would be reopened, and institutions revise slowly when the cost of having been wrong is borne by the institution itself.

passages.title: Banking the Seeds
passages.text:
Agriculture depends on genetic variety it no longer widely plants. Across the twentieth century, farming consolidated onto a small number of high-yielding varieties, and the thousands of local landraces that preceded them fell out of cultivation. A crop grown as a handful of genetically similar varieties across a continent is efficient and is also uniformly vulnerable: a disease that defeats one plant's defences defeats them all.

Seed banks exist to hold what is no longer grown. Samples are dried, sealed and stored at low temperature, where many species remain viable for decades. The largest facilities hold hundreds of thousands of accessions, and a facility in the Arctic operates as a backup of backups, holding duplicates deposited by other banks against the loss of the original collection — a provision that has already been used at least once, when a regional bank was destroyed in conflict.

Storage is not preservation, and the distinction is where most of the difficulty lies. Seeds lose viability gradually even in ideal conditions, so every accession must periodically be grown out, allowed to set new seed, and returned to store. This regeneration is labour-intensive, requires land and expertise, and must avoid the sample drifting genetically through selection in the growing environment. Backlogs of accessions overdue for regeneration are common and are the principal way collections quietly degrade.

Documentation determines value in the same way it does for museums. An accession with recorded origin, altitude, soil and the practices of the farmers who maintained it can be searched for useful traits; the same seed without that record is a bag of unknown material. Much older collecting recorded little, and the knowledge held by the communities that developed those varieties was frequently not collected at all.

The legal position has become the sector's most contested area. Varieties developed over generations by farming communities have been used to breed commercial cultivars, and the question of what obligation flows back has produced international agreements that are complex, incompletely implemented and read very differently by the parties to them. Some countries have restricted access to their genetic material in response, which protects a legitimate interest and simultaneously slows the exchange that makes collections useful.

A practical criticism deserves more attention than it receives. Seeds in storage do not evolve, while the pests and climates they must eventually face do. A variety returned to cultivation after fifty years enters conditions it has not adapted to for fifty years. This is the argument for on-farm conservation — varieties maintained in cultivation by the communities using them, continuing to adapt. It is harder to fund, harder to audit, and produces no visible facility to open, which is a poor reason for it to remain the smaller half of the effort.
